modules.title: Cloud concepts scenario depth
modules.summary: Scenario-based deepening for cloud benefits and service models.

lessons.title: Cloud benefits beyond scale: reliability, predictability, governance, and manageability
lessons.summary: Deepens cloud benefits that the existing path only introduces.
learningObjectives: Explain reliability, predictability, governance, and manageability benefits in cloud scenarios
Identify controls such as tags, policies, RBAC, alerts, and Advisor recommendations
Distinguish managing cloud resources from managing resources with cloud tools
lessons.explanation: Reliability, predictability, security, governance, and manageability are benefits only when a team uses the right controls. Reliability means designing for recovery. Predictability means planning from known behavior, monitoring, and tested changes. Security protects identities, data, and resources, while governance applies standards such as policies, tags, and access reviews. Manageability has two sides: **of the cloud**, using tools to deploy and monitor resources, and **in the cloud**, because the provider handles physical facilities and many platform operations. In scenarios, match the business clue to the benefit: failure recovery is reliability, approved regions are governance, dashboards and automation are manageability.

terminology.definition: Recovering from failures and continuing to operate.
Planning from expected service behavior, monitoring, and tested changes.
Protecting identities, data, applications, and resources.
Applying standards such as policy, tags, and access reviews.
Using cloud tools to deploy, monitor, automate, and organize resources.

lessons.businessScenario: Tailwind Traders is launching ticket sales for a charity concert. Marketing wants a fast release, finance wants every cost tied to a campaign, and security wants the site to survive routine component problems without becoming a free-for-all.
lessons.technicalExample: The team deploys the app in an approved region, adds owner and campaign tags, assigns least-privilege roles, creates availability and cost alerts, and reviews Azure Advisor recommendations after the first event.

misconception.myth: Reliability, governance, and manageability appear automatically just because a workload runs in Azure.
misconception.reality: Azure supplies controls such as regions, policy, tags, identity, and monitoring, but the customer must select and configure them for the workload.

lessons.examTakeaway: If the scenario says survive failure, choose reliability; if it says approved locations, ownership, or standards, choose governance; if it says dashboards, automation, or less operations work, choose manageability.
lessons.recap: Deepens cloud benefits that the existing path only introduces.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Imagine a concert venue: the building has exits, signs, guards, and a control room, but the event team still assigns seats, checks tickets, and watches the crowd.
lessons.anotherExample: A library portal uses policy to keep resources in approved regions, tags each resource by branch, and alerts staff when response time or spending moves outside the expected range.

data.title: Cloud benefit clues for the concert site

columns.title: Reliability
points: Ticket checkout should continue through routine component issues

columns.title: Governance and security
points: Owner tags and least privilege are required

columns.title: Manageability
points: The team reduces physical infrastructure work

data.title: Concert launch triage
data.instructions: Match each request to the strongest cloud benefit.

items.prompt: “Keep selling tickets if a component fails.”

flashcards.back: A requirement to keep working or recover after a failure.
A requirement for approved regions, tags, standards, or ownership.
Using Azure tools to deploy, scale, automate, and monitor resources.
Provider-handled operations such as physical datacenter maintenance.
A requirement for expected behavior, measured trends, and fewer surprises.

knowledgeCheck.stem: A payment application is deployed across multiple Azure availability zones so it can keep processing orders if one datacenter has a hardware issue. Which cloud benefit is the primary goal?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Reliability is the benefit focused on continuing to operate or recovering when a component or location has a problem. The zone design supports that goal by avoiding a single point of failure.

options.explanation: Reliability addresses availability and recovery during failures.
Elasticity adjusts capacity as demand changes; the stem is about failure tolerance.
Cost management tracks and optimizes spending but does not describe surviving a datacenter problem.
SaaS is a service model, not a cloud benefit for resilient architecture.

knowledgeCheck.stem: Which **two** Azure controls help an organization keep cloud resources consistently classified and deployed only in approved locations?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Tags and Azure Policy are governance controls. Tags add business metadata, and policy can evaluate or enforce allowed settings such as permitted regions.

options.text: Resource tags such as Department and Environment
options.explanation: Tags classify resources for ownership, reporting, automation, and cost analysis.

options.text: Azure Policy definitions that restrict allowed regions
options.explanation: Azure Policy can audit, deny, or remediate resources that do not meet rules such as allowed locations.
VM size changes capacity and performance; it does not standardize metadata or allowed locations.
Archive tier is a storage lifecycle choice, not a governance control for resource placement.

sources.title: Study guide for Exam AZ-900: Microsoft Azure Fundamentals
Describe the benefits of using cloud services

knowledgeCheck.stem: True or false: A workload that has a tested recovery plan and redundant components is using cloud reliability practices.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The statement is true because reliability is about designing and operating a workload so it can withstand failures and recover within expected timeframes.

options.explanation: Correct. Redundant components and tested recovery plans help a workload withstand failures and recover within expected targets.
Choosing False misses that reliability practices include redundancy, failover planning, and recovery testing.

knowledgeCheck.stem: Match each requirement to the cloud benefit or management concept it best represents.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Each match is based on the business clue: failure continuity maps to reliability, approved standards map to governance, spend alerts map to cost management, and automation dashboards map to manageability.

prompts.text: Keep the checkout API available during routine component failure
Deny creation of resources outside approved Azure regions
Notify owners when monthly spending approaches a budget
Use dashboards and scripts to operate resources consistently

explanations.p1: Reliability focuses on continuity and recovery when components fail.
explanations.p2: Governance applies organizational rules such as approved regions.
explanations.p3: Budgets and alerts help teams monitor and control cloud spend.
explanations.p4: Manageability uses tools, automation, and monitoring to operate resources.

knowledgeCheck.scenario: Contoso is preparing a short-term ticketing site. Finance wants each resource charged to a campaign, security wants deployments limited to two approved regions, and operations wants alerts for availability issues.
knowledgeCheck.stem: What should Contoso configure first to satisfy the governance requirements before the site is deployed?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Tags and Azure Policy address the stated governance needs before resources are created: tags support campaign cost tracking, and policy can restrict deployment locations.

options.text: Define required tags and an Azure Policy assignment for allowed regions
options.explanation: This combines metadata standards with enforcement of approved deployment locations.

options.text: Increase every virtual machine to the largest available size
options.explanation: Larger VMs do not add campaign metadata or region enforcement.

options.text: Move the app to SaaS so the business cannot configure governance
options.explanation: SaaS changes responsibility boundaries but does not directly configure Azure tags or policy for this deployment.

options.text: Choose archive storage for all ticketing transactions
options.explanation: Archive storage is for rarely accessed blobs, not governance of compute and app resources.

lessons.title: Choosing IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS from scenario clues
lessons.summary: Adds scenario practice for cloud service types and shared responsibility.
learningObjectives: Compare IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS by customer control and provider responsibility
Choose a service type from OS control, custom code, or finished app clues
Explain how shared responsibility changes from VMs to SaaS apps
lessons.explanation: IaaS gives the customer the most control, including guest OS and installed software. It fits legacy apps, special OS settings, and lift-and-shift. PaaS lets developers deploy custom code while the provider manages more of the platform. SaaS is a finished application. Shared responsibility changes as you move from IaaS to SaaS, but customers always keep responsibility for data decisions, access, and business configuration. Read for control, speed, and management effort: OS control points to IaaS, code without servers points to PaaS, and ready-to-use apps point to SaaS.

terminology.definition: Infrastructure as a service: customer manages guest OS, apps, data, and configuration.
Platform as a service: developers deploy code while the provider manages more platform operations.
Software as a service: users consume a finished application.
The OS inside a virtual machine that the customer patches and configures in IaaS.
Data, access, and business configuration choices that remain with the customer.

lessons.businessScenario: Woodgrove Bank is sorting three requests: a loan app with a custom Windows service, a new customer API that developers want to ship weekly, and a standard HR case-management tool.
lessons.technicalExample: Architects keep the loan app on Azure VMs for OS control, host the new API on App Service, and subscribe to a SaaS HR tool while managing employee access and data-retention settings.

misconception.myth: Choosing SaaS means Woodgrove can ignore access, data, and configuration choices.
misconception.reality: SaaS reduces application operations, but Woodgrove still owns user assignments, data decisions, compliance configuration, and business process choices.

lessons.examTakeaway: OS-level control points to IaaS, custom code with less server work points to PaaS, and a ready-to-use business application points to SaaS.
lessons.recap: Adds scenario practice for cloud service types and shared responsibility.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of lunch: IaaS is renting a kitchen, PaaS is using a prepared kitchen counter, and SaaS is ordering the finished meal.
lessons.anotherExample: A retailer runs a licensed inventory app on VMs, deploys its loyalty API to a managed app platform, and uses a SaaS help-desk product for support tickets.

data.title: Shortcut
data.body: Ask what the team wants to manage: machines, code, or only app configuration.

flashcards.back: The scenario requires OS control, custom drivers, or lift-and-shift.
The scenario wants custom code without managing servers directly.
The scenario wants a finished application for users.
Manage users, data, and business configuration.
IaaS gives most control; SaaS gives least infrastructure management.

knowledgeCheck.stem: A legacy inventory application requires administrators to install custom agents, change the guest operating system, and control patch timing. Which cloud service model best fits this requirement?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: IaaS provides virtual machines where the customer has the most control over the guest operating system and installed software, which matches the legacy application requirement.

options.explanation: IaaS gives customers VM-level control over the guest OS and installed agents.
PaaS reduces OS administration and is better when the team can deploy code without managing the guest OS.
SaaS is a finished application and normally does not allow guest OS changes.
Consumption billing is a cost model, not a service model for OS control.

sources.title: Study guide for Exam AZ-900: Microsoft Azure Fundamentals
Describe Cloud Service Types

knowledgeCheck.stem: Which **two** statements correctly describe shared responsibility when moving from IaaS toward SaaS?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The provider takes on more platform and application operation as the model moves toward SaaS, but the customer still owns data, identities, access decisions, and business configuration.

options.text: The cloud provider manages more of the underlying platform in PaaS than in IaaS.
options.explanation: PaaS shifts runtime and platform maintenance away from the customer.

options.text: Customers still make data governance and access decisions in SaaS.
options.explanation: Even with SaaS, customers manage users, data, permissions, and business settings.

options.text: SaaS gives the customer the most control over the guest operating system.
options.explanation: Guest OS control is associated with IaaS, not SaaS.

options.text: In IaaS, the provider owns application code and data classification.
options.explanation: Application code and data decisions remain customer responsibilities in IaaS.

sources.title: Study guide for Exam AZ-900: Microsoft Azure Fundamentals
Describe Cloud Service Types

knowledgeCheck.stem: True or false: A provider-hosted email system that users access in a browser is usually an example of SaaS.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The statement is true because SaaS delivers a complete application for users while the provider manages the application platform.

options.explanation: Correct. Browser-based provider-hosted email is a complete application delivered to users, which is the SaaS model.
Choosing False misses that SaaS means consuming a finished provider-managed application rather than managing the platform yourself.

knowledgeCheck.stem: Match each scenario to the cloud service model or responsibility concept it best demonstrates.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The matches separate VM control, managed application platforms, complete applications, and responsibilities that remain with the customer.

prompts.text: Administrators patch the guest OS on an Azure VM
Developers deploy web code while Azure manages the web server platform
Employees use a provider-hosted HR application through a browser
The business classifies data and grants user access

explanations.p1: Guest OS patching is a typical customer task with IaaS VMs.
explanations.p2: PaaS hosts custom code while reducing platform administration.
explanations.p3: SaaS is a complete application delivered by a provider.
explanations.p4: Data classification and user access decisions remain customer responsibilities.

knowledgeCheck.scenario: Fabrikam is modernizing a custom customer API. Developers need to publish their own code, but they do not want to manage operating system patches or web server maintenance.
knowledgeCheck.stem: Which service model best matches the API hosting requirement?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: PaaS is the best fit because it supports custom application code while shifting operating system and platform maintenance to the provider.

options.explanation: PaaS lets developers deploy custom code with less infrastructure and OS management.
IaaS would leave more VM and guest OS maintenance with the customer.
SaaS is a finished application and would not normally host Fabrikam-owned API code.
The requirement asks for a cloud service model, and on-premises hosting keeps full infrastructure responsibility.
